name: Mount Erebus
title: Mount Erebus: Lava Lake, Last Eruption, Height & Facts
description: Mount Erebus in Antarctica has been erupting since at least {cur_start}, with a lava lake in its summit crater. Height, type, location and full eruption record.

lede: Mount Erebus is an Antarctic volcano with a lake of molten rock at its top. NASA calls it the southernmost active volcano on Earth,[[nasa]] and by the Smithsonian’s record it has been erupting since at least {cur_start}.[[gvp]]
answer: **Mount Erebus is erupting now.** The Smithsonian lists its current eruption as running since {cur_since}, and it was still going at the last update on {cur_last}.[[gvp]] The eruption is a lava lake in the summit crater of this **{summit_ft} ft ({summit_m} m)** stratovolcano on Ross Island, Antarctica.[[nasa]]

paras: Mount Erebus is on Ross Island, off the coast of West Antarctica, at {coords}.[[nasa]][[gvp]] McMurdo Station is about 22 miles (35 km) away.[[nasa]] It is one of {n_country} volcanoes in [Antarctica](/volcanoes-in-antarctica) on the Smithsonian’s Holocene list.[[gvp]]
Yes, by the Smithsonian’s record. It lists Erebus as erupting since **{cur_since}**, and the eruption was still going at its last update on {cur_last}.[[gvp]] That makes {cur_years} years.
Only {older_count_word} eruptions the Smithsonian lists as continuing began earlier: {older}.[[gvp]]

sections.h: Does Mount Erebus have a lava lake?
paras: Yes. A lava lake sits in the summit crater and has been active **since at least 1972**. NASA calls it one of only a few long-lived lava lakes on Earth.[[nasa]]
The lake churns constantly and now and then throws out bombs of molten rock.[[nasa]] Bursts like that are called Strombolian eruptions, after Stromboli in Italy.[[nps]]
Why the lake has lasted so long is an open question. NASA reports recent research suggesting that the magma holds little water, which makes it less volatile near the surface.[[nasa]]

sections.h: What type of volcano is Mount Erebus?
paras: Mount Erebus is a **[stratovolcano](/types-of-volcanoes)**: a steep-sided cone built from lava flows and the debris of explosive eruptions.[[nasa]][[usgsgloss]] The Smithsonian lists its main rock as {rock}.[[gvp]]
It stands in a rift zone, where the crust has been stretched thin and magma rises to the surface through faults.[[nasa]]
Mount Erebus is **{summit_ft} ft ({summit_m} m)** above sea level.[[gvp]] It rises straight from the sea: Ross Island is made of Erebus and several other volcanoes.[[nasa]]

sections.h: How many times has Mount Erebus erupted?
paras: The Smithsonian’s list has **{n_all} confirmed eruptions** of Mount Erebus. Written reports account for {n_written} of them, starting in {since_year}; the other {n_other} are dated from rocks.[[gvp]]
The volcano was first seen that same year, by James Clark Ross of the British Royal Navy on his Antarctic voyage. Erebus and its neighbor Mount Terror were named after his expedition’s ships.[[nasa]]

None of the {n_all} eruptions is rated above VEI {max_vei} on the [Volcanic Explosivity Index](/volcanic-explosivity-index).[[gvp]] NOAA’s database of significant eruptions has no entry for Erebus.[[noaa]]
The Smithsonian’s record for Mount Erebus has **{n_all} confirmed eruptions**. Most have a start date and no end date: the reports come from expeditions that sailed on.[[gvp]]
